We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times [22]. Zip codes are postal codes used by the U.S. postal service to identify geographic delivery areas. These regions are often used as a proxy for local community characteristics [23]. Election results included the numbers of votes for the Democratic and Republican candidate (Biden and Trump, respectively) as well as the total number of votes for each Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) code. Political climate for each participant was determined by matching FIPS codes to corresponding zip codes. In cases where a zip code included multiple FIPS codes, data was averaged across these FIPS. Using the FIPS data for each zip code, we calculated the percent of Republican votes by dividing the number of Republican votes by the total number of votes (multiplied by 100). Vaccine hesitancy (i.e., negative attitudes toward vaccination) was measured using the seven items from the Attitudes towards Adult Vaccination Scale [24], which assesses the perceived value of vaccines in general. We modified the items to assess attitudes specifically toward the COVID-19 vaccine [e.g., I fear the potential impact of the COVID-19 vaccine on my health in the future, I believe that the benefits of COVID-19 vaccination outweigh the potential risks (reverse-scored)]. Each item was rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from disagree strongly (1) to agree strongly (5). These items were averaged to form a vaccine hesitancy scale. Booster hesitancy was assessed using items from a 2022 survey on COVID-19 booster hesitancy [25].

In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective. This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth. Because the conventional assumption in much of the adolescent health literature, that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study, which may also mean that common network intervention strategies aimed at reducing substance use may not be as effective as previously thought [4,5,10].

Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects—indicating whether individuals who use substances are more likely to receive or initiate friendships—were almost entirely non-significant across all three schools and substances. The only exception was a positive sender effect for alcohol use in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05), suggesting a tendency for alcohol-using adolescents to initiate more friendship nominations in that setting.

Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties. Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity.

The ERGM results revealed strong and consistent endogenous structural effects across all three schools (Table 3). Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations. Similarly, the positive coefficients for closed triads (transitivity) and negative coefficients for two‑path confirmed that triadic closure—the process by which friends of friends become friends—is a fundamental organizing principle within these AI adolescent networks.

Homophily effects provided further evidence of distinct relational logics. Gender and grade homophily were consistently significant across all schools (AME = 0.008–0.058, all p < 0.001), indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation, as extensively documented in the broader adolescent literature [9,12].

Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects—indicating whether individuals who use substances are more likely to receive or initiate friendships—were almost entirely non-significant across all three schools and substances. The only exception was a positive sender effect for alcohol use in School C (AME = 0.015, p < 0.05), suggesting a tendency for alcohol-using adolescents to initiate more friendship nominations in that setting.

Depression likewise showed no substantively meaningful associations with friendship formation among AI adolescents, unlike the negative receiver effects and depression homophily commonly observed in non-AI populations [46]; the isolated statistically significant estimates were negligible in magnitude (AME < 0.001).

AI identity homophily was consistently non-significant across all schools. This null finding, while seemingly counterintuitive given the cultural emphasis on tribal belonging, is consistent with several contextual considerations. First, in AI-majority schools, racial identity is a near-universal attribute; with nearly all students identifying as AI, there is insufficient variation in racial category for identity to differentiate friendship choices. Homophily on AI identity is theoretically redundant when almost all potential friends share the same racial background.

The findings of this study are not without their limitations. First, we recognize that the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation. The history, policies, geography, and culture of this reservation all intersect with network formation and maintenance patterns. Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context. Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.

In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude [6,11,13,22] (see Table 1 for a summary of prior findings). By contrast, in our AI-majority sample, substance use showed no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools.
